Let \(K\) be the number of \(+1\)'s, so \(S=2K-12\). For any admissible law, every polynomial in \(S\) of degree at most \(8\) has the same expectation as under \(U\).

Define
\[
q(K)=\frac{(K-1)(K-2)(K-3)(K-4)(K-8)(K-9)(K-10)(K-11)}{14400}.
\]
Then \(q(6)=1\), while \(q(K)\ge 0\) for every \(K\in\{0,\dots,12\}\), and \(q(K)=0\) except at \(K=0,5,6,7,12\). Hence
\[
\mathbf 1_{\{K=6\}}\le q(K).
\]
Since \(q\) has degree \(8\),
\[
\mu(S=0)=\mu(K=6)\le \mathbb E_\mu q(K)=\mathbb E_U q(K).
\]
Now
\[
\mathbb E_U q(K)
=\frac{1}{2^{12}}\left(2\cdot \frac{66}{5}+2\binom{12}{5}\frac35+\binom{12}{6}\right)
=\frac{297}{640}.
\]

Equality is attained by the density
\[
f(x)=\frac{d\bar\mu}{dU}(x)
=1+\frac{R(x)(74-S(x)^2)}{70}.
\]
Indeed \(f\ge 0\) on all possible values of \(S\), and
\[
f-1=\frac1{70}R(74-S^2)
\]
has Fourier degree only \(10\) and \(12\), so all Fourier coefficients of degrees \(1,\dots,8\) vanish. Thus the resulting law is unbiased and \(8\)-wise independent.

Equality in the dual bound forces the symmetrized law to put no mass on \(K=0,5,7,12\). Together with the nine moment constraints of degrees \(0,\dots,8\), the remaining nine masses are uniquely determined, so every maximizing law has the same permutation symmetrization.

\[
\boxed{\left(\frac{297}{640},\; x\mapsto 1+\frac{R(x)(74-S(x)^2)}{70}\right)}
\]
